title: The Jury Trial Is Under Attack
author: Erin Hagood
content:
![The Jury Trial Is Under
Attack](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/AP26237513831455.jpg)

After a Massachusetts judge announced a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case on
September 4, it didn't take long for the media to turn its focus from the
trial to the jurors. We learned that the jury was hung by a single holdout
juror who wanted to convict Clancy. We also soon discovered that the jury
deliberations had been heated. According to the majority of the jury,**** the
holdout juror stated during deliberations that he did hold reasonable doubt as
to Clancy's mental state at the time of the murders, yet he refused to apply
the legal standard for non-responsibility. For his part, the holdout juror
claims that he was essentially bullied by the other jurors, who [_repeatedly
cut him
off_](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Non2BzVYVmg__;!!BDUfV1Et5lrpZQ!XoZZanwvgXIz61XrdHd4PkoiobxkJEZFfta-8APxa5qRON6J7wjJcWPy3jfKDDCCVvlTSq1d5sGlm1p86zuKfw8Nj12WOxdk$&ref=compactmag.com),
and that he never had any doubt as to Clancy's guilt.

The veracity of these claims may determine Clancy's fate. Clancy's lawyer has
asked the judge for permission to probe the holdout juror for possible
misconduct, and on Tuesday, the court heard arguments concerning a motion to
dismiss all charges. If there is a retrial, the media interviews with the
jurors will serve as market research for the prosecution and defense to tinker
with their theories and modify their jury selection strategies. And given the
attention the case has received, assembling an impartial retrial jury will be
a serious challenge. In the meantime, the holdout juror has reportedly
received death threats and has been hiding out in an undisclosed location.

The Clancy jury is hardly the first panel to face public criticism in recent
years. The juries that acquitted Kyle Rittenhouse, convicted Derek Chauvin,
and freed Casey Anthony, to name a few, were also subjected to public
scrutiny. It is a good moment to ask ourselves: What are juries for? Why do we
trust twelve regular people with decisions of freedom, justice, life and
death?
